slides.title: Lecture 4: Ensembles
slides.summary: Lecture 4 introduces the topic of ensembles within the broader context of machine learning and inductive inference. This session, presented by Sieben Bocklandt, utilizes slide decks originally developed by Jesse Davis for the Principles of Machine Learning course to explore these concepts.

slides.title: – Deep understanding of how ensemble algorithms work
slides.summary: This lecture aims to provide a deep understanding of ensemble algorithms by contrasting team-based models with single-player approaches. Key topics include voting, stacking, bagging, random forests, boosting (specifically AdaBoost and XGBoost), and error-correcting output codes. Beyond mastering these techniques, students must grasp their respective strengths and weaknesses, understand the intuitive reasons why ensembles succeed, and learn how to apply them for tasks like multi-class classification using binary classifiers.

slides.title: – Voting, stacking, bagging and random forests
slides.summary: This section outlines key ensemble methods, including voting, stacking, bagging, random forests, AdaBoost, and XGBoost, alongside topics on manipulating inputs/outputs, the rationale for why ensembles work, and their applications. The professor illustrates the concept of ensembles using a camera analogy, where installing multiple cameras to track movement from different angles provides a comprehensive view, similar to how combining models improves performance. This serves as a general introduction to ensemble techniques.

This approach treats the collection as a "team" or "band" of models to integrate diverse classifications for more robust decision-making.

slides.title: – An ensemble model is a predictive model that is a combination of several different predictive
slides.summary: An ensemble model combines several different predictive models to form a single, more robust predictor. These are classified as homogeneous ensembles when they use the same type of models, or heterogeneous ensembles when they integrate different types. This approach often yields higher accuracy than any individual constituent model, operating on the principle that "two know more than one."

slides.title: – An ensemble model is a predictive model that is a combination of several different
slides.summary: An ensemble model combines several predictive models to achieve greater accuracy than any single constituent, operating on the principle that "two know more than one". These ensembles are classified as homogeneous when using the same model type in multiple ways, or heterogeneous when combining different model types. While this approach improves predictions by adding redundancy and correcting errors through diverse outputs, it raises critical questions regarding how to generate models with distinct mistakes, which specific algorithms to consider, and how to effectively combine their individual predictions into a final result.

slides.title: Use multiple models
slides.summary: Using multiple models allows their predictions to be combined in an ensemble.

slides.title: – Assume we have k classifiers M1, M2, …, Mk
slides.summary: Majority voting aggregates predictions from $k$ classifiers ($M_1, \dots, M_k$) by selecting the class predicted most frequently for a given instance $x$. While conceptually trivial, this method is effective; its theoretical analysis assumes all classifiers share accuracy $p$ and make independent errors. Although the independence assumption is not always perfectly valid in practice, it serves as a foundational premise for understanding why ensemble voting improves performance.

slides.title: – The question is difficult to answer in general, but we can analyze what
slides.summary: While the general question is difficult, analysis under simplifying assumptions shows that combining independent classifiers with equal accuracy $p$ significantly boosts performance. Assuming mistakes are statistically independent—meaning one model's error does not influence another's—adding more models increases overall accuracy; for instance, individual accuracy of 0.8 rises to 0.896 with three classifiers, 0.988 with eleven, and 0.999 with twenty-one.

slides.title: – We can prove that voting helps if we have equally good models that make
slides.summary: Voting ensembles are provably effective when combining equally good models that make independent mistakes, though adding more models generally works under these heavy assumptions. However, if errors are correlated or model accuracies differ, no theoretical proof exists, necessitating experimental validation to confirm performance. While the core concept of voting remains valid, this limitation motivates alternative approaches like stacking, where base learner predictions serve as input for a meta-learner to generate final outputs.

slides.title: – Use the votes as the input of a new learner
slides.summary: In stacking, the predictions or votes generated by multiple base learners serve as the input features for a new meta-learner. This process effectively functions as a data transformation, where the original dataset is converted into a new representation composed of these learner outputs before being fed to the final model for prediction.

slides.title: Use the same algorithm,
slides.summary: To improve model performance or adapt to new contexts, maintain the identical underlying algorithm while varying the training data used. This approach isolates the impact of data composition on outcomes without introducing changes from the model architecture itself. By keeping the algorithm constant, any observed differences in results can be directly attributed to the specific variations in the dataset provided during training.

slides.title: – Goal: multiple models that make different mistakes
slides.summary: To generate multiple models that make different mistakes from a single training set, we use bootstrap replicates by sampling $|S|$ examples with replacement to create new datasets ($S'$). This process allows specific instances to appear multiple times in a replicate while others are omitted entirely, as illustrated by the example where one item is selected twice and another is excluded. Consequently, each resulting model trains on a slightly different data distribution, enabling the ensemble to capture diverse error patterns despite originating from one source dataset.

slides.title: – Claim: 63.2% chance example 𝑥is in a bootstrap replicate 𝑆’ with size |S|=n
slides.summary: There is a 63.2% probability that any specific example $x$ appears in a bootstrap replicate $S'$ of size $n$, leaving a 36.8% chance it is excluded. This result derives from calculating the probability that $x$ is not selected for any of the $n$ positions, which is $(1 - 1/n)^n$, and subtracting this from one. As $n$ increases, this value asymptotically approaches $1 - 1/e \approx 0.632$. This inherent sampling variation ensures different training sets across replicates, enabling the creation of diverse models for ensemble combination.

slides.title: – Given: Data set S, integer T
slides.summary: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) constructs an ensemble by generating $T$ bootstrap replicates from a dataset $S$, training a separate learner $h_t$ on each replicate, and combining their predictions via an unweighted vote. For instance, if three models predict true, false, and false respectively, the final output is determined by majority vote as false. This process leverages sampling to create diverse models that are aggregated to improve overall prediction stability.

slides.title: – Bagging works with any learner in principle
slides.summary: While bagging can theoretically be applied to any learner, it is most effective for unstable algorithms where minor training data variations cause significant output changes. Examples of unstable learners include decision trees, neural networks, rule learning algorithms, and 1-nearest neighbor (1NN), whereas linear regression, kNN with $k>1$, and linear threshold algorithms are stable. Bagging benefits unstable learners by using sampling to exclude noisy data points, thereby simplifying the classification task and preventing the model from overfitting to specific outliers.

slides.title: – Suppose your data looks like this:
slides.summary: Bagging improves model performance by using bootstrap replicates to generate training data that excludes noisy examples, which often forces learners to expend less effort fitting outliers. This technique is most effective with unstable learners because small perturbations in the input data—caused by including or excluding specific examples during sampling—result in significant changes to the model output. Aggregating these diverse models leverages these variations to create a more robust final prediction.

slides.title: – A variant of Bagging
slides.summary: Random Forests are a variant of Bagging designed to further decorrelate models by introducing feature randomness during tree construction. For each of T bootstrap replicates of the dataset, a decision tree is built without pruning; at every recursive split, the algorithm selects n features at random and chooses the best among them as the root for that subtree. This specific constraint on feature selection reduces model correlation compared to standard Bagging while maintaining the ensemble's robustness.

slides.title: – Increasing n increases
slides.summary: Increasing the number of trees ($n$) creates a trade-off: it raises correlation among trees due to shared features (negative), but simultaneously improves individual tree accuracy by increasing the probability of generating accurate replicates (positive). Because these opposing effects may stabilize at a specific point, a tuning or validation set is required to identify the optimal $n$. Overall, random forests are computationally fast, handle large feature sets effectively through sampling, substantially reduce overfitting, and remain a gold standard that performs exceptionally well in practice.

slides.title: – Given Dataset S, integer T
slides.summary: Random Forests extend bagging by building T decision trees on bootstrap replicates of dataset S, introducing randomness at each split by selecting n features without replacement and choosing the best among them, which may exclude the globally optimal split. Trees are grown fully without pruning to maximize variance reduction through ensemble aggregation. An alternative approach, Extremely Randomized Trees (Extra Trees), further increases randomness by selecting random split points for the chosen features rather than optimizing the split value, trading individual model accuracy for greater diversity within the forest.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: To evaluate how well each learned model generalizes, an alternative method called out-of-bag error is used. For every example in the database, predictions are gathered only from models that did not include that specific example during training. The final error metric is calculated by taking the majority vote of these independent predictions, comparing them to the true labels, and averaging the resulting errors across all examples.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: To evaluate how well learned models generalize, the out-of-bag error method assesses performance using data points excluded from training. For each database example, identify all models that did not train on it—occurring with approximately 37% probability in bootstrap replicates—and aggregate their predictions via majority vote. The final error metric is calculated by comparing these votes against true labels and averaging the resulting errors across all examples.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: To evaluate how well each learned model generalizes using out-of-bag error, the process examines every example in the database by identifying all models that were not trained on it. These specific models provide predictions for the example via a majority vote, which is then compared against the true label to determine the error. The final evaluation metric is calculated by taking the average of these individual errors across the dataset.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: To evaluate how well learned models generalize, calculate the Out-of-Bag error by testing each database example against only those models that were not trained on it. For every example, aggregate the predictions of these excluded models via a majority vote and compare the result to the true label. The final generalization metric is the average of these errors across all examples, providing an alternative evaluation method that avoids using training data for validation.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: To evaluate how well each learned model generalizes, the out-of-bag error method assesses performance on examples excluded from a specific model's training set. For every database example, predictions are aggregated via majority vote from all models that did not train on it, and these collective predictions are compared against the true labels. The final evaluation metric is the average of these errors across all examples, providing an alternative assessment of model generalization without requiring separate validation data.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: To evaluate how well each learned model generalizes, the out-of-bag error method assesses performance without requiring a separate test set. For every example in the database, predictions are aggregated from all models that did not train on that specific instance using a majority vote. The final evaluation metric is the average of the errors resulting from comparing these aggregated predictions against the true labels.

slides.title: – How well does each learned model generalize?
slides.summary: Out-of-bag error evaluates model generalization by testing each instance only on models that did not train on it, using a majority vote of their predictions against the true label. For example, if three models predict an unseen yellow instance as negative while its actual label is positive, this counts as an error; averaging these errors across all instances yields the out-of-bag metric. Minimizing this error indicates strong generalization because the models correctly predict data they have never encountered, with results converging through repeated resampling in methods like random forests.

slides.title: Learn from previous
slides.summary: Boosting trains successive learners to focus on examples that previous learners classified incorrectly.

slides.title: – Typically, we want “strong learners”, i.e., high chance to get small error rate
slides.summary: While strong learners offer high accuracy with minimal error, they are difficult to train; therefore, boosting iteratively combines weak learners—models only slightly better than random guessing—to form a robust additive model. Each new model is greedily added to specifically correct the mispredictions of previous ones by adjusting weights, which increases the overall margin and confidence. This process allows test accuracy to improve even after training error reaches zero, avoiding the typical overfitting seen in other complex models.

slides.title: – Works for binary classification problems
slides.summary: AdaBoost addresses binary classification by iteratively learning an additive model where each new weak learner focuses on examples misclassified by previous models. The algorithm re-weights training data to increase the importance of incorrect predictions, ensuring subsequent classifiers prioritize difficult cases. Final predictions result from a weighted vote where more accurate models receive higher coefficients ($\alpha$), allowing the ensemble magnitude to reflect confidence levels beyond simple class labels.

slides.title: Given: Training examples E, Integer T
slides.summary: The AdaBoost algorithm initializes training examples with equal weights and iteratively trains simple classifiers $h_t$ for $T$ rounds. In each iteration, it calculates the weighted error $\epsilon_t$, determines the classifier's voting strength $\alpha_t$, and then increases the weights of misclassified examples while decreasing those correctly classified to prioritize difficult cases for subsequent learners. After normalizing these weights to sum to one, the new classifier and its strength are added to the ensemble, ensuring that models performing well receive higher influence in the final prediction.

slides.title: – Expect: Training error drops to 0, but test error increases
slides.summary: While it is typically expected that training error drops to zero while test error increases due to overfitting, the observed results contradict this trend. Even after 1000 rounds, the test error remains stable and continues to decrease even after the training error has reached zero. This phenomenon demonstrates that increasing the number of rounds does not necessarily degrade generalization in this specific context.

slides.title: – Key idea: Error only measures if classification is correct, but confidence of
slides.summary: While standard error only measures classification correctness, prediction confidence is critical for difficult examples near decision boundaries. Confidence is quantified by the margin, calculated as the difference between weighted positive and negative votes, where large margins indicate strong agreement among weak learners rather than increased model complexity. Theoretically, maximizing these margins yields tighter bounds on generalization error, ensuring the model takes a decisive stance (e.g., high confidence in failure) rather than hovering uncertainly at the border.

slides.title: – Continuous search method
slides.summary: Gradient descent is an iterative algorithm used in continuous search methods to optimize a model by starting with initial values and progressively improving them toward a goal. The process involves calculating the gradient to determine the direction of improvement, taking a step, and re-evaluating; if steps are too large and overshoot the target, recalculating the gradient allows the algorithm to correct course and find the optimal model fit.

slides.title: – Extreme gradient boosting
slides.summary: Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) extends additive ensemble models by training each new decision tree component to take a step in the direction of the negative gradient, effectively minimizing error iteratively. Although considered a niche concept inspired by deep learning principles, XGBoost remains exceptionally performant and is currently regarded as the gold standard for tabular data learning, often outperforming large neural networks on such datasets.

slides.title: Change the output labels
slides.summary: Changing output labels changes the names shown for classes, not the underlying predictions.

slides.title: – Given k>2 classes: A B C …
slides.summary: For multiclass problems with $k>2$ classes, the one-vs-rest strategy trains $k$ binary classifiers where each distinguishes one positive class from all others, selecting the final prediction based on the highest confidence score. Alternatively, an ensemble approach splits classes into multiple sets to create redundancy; this evolves into error-correcting output codes, where each class is represented by a unique bit code across $t$ models. This coding scheme allows the system to tolerate individual model errors and correctly identify the class even if some predictions are incorrect.

slides.title: – Encode by partition output labels in 2 subsets, create log(k) models
slides.summary: To address multiclass problems, encode output labels by partitioning them into two subsets for each binary model, requiring approximately log(k) models where k is the number of classes. This approach systematically groups labels (e.g., A,B,C,D vs E,F,G,H) across different partitions to distinguish all categories. Additionally, creating more than the minimum log(k) models introduces redundancy, functioning as "error-correcting codes" to improve robustness against individual model errors.

slides.title: – Ensemble method for multiclass problems
slides.summary: This ensemble method addresses multiclass problems by constructing a T-bit codeword for each class to enable error correction. For every binary classifier $h_i$, the corresponding bit in a class's codeword is set to 1 if that class is assigned to the positive label set, or 0 if it is assigned to the negative label set. The process involves iterating through T steps where labels are partitioned into two disjoint sets, and a model is trained on these new binary classifications.

slides.title: – Given example 𝑥, create bit vector ℎ(𝑥) of length T where the ith bit:
slides.summary: In Error-Correcting Output Codes, given an example $x$, construct a bit vector $h(x)$ of length $T$ where the $i$-th bit is set to 1 if the base learner $h_i(x)$ predicts positive, and 0 if it predicts negative. The final classification is determined by identifying the class whose code has the smallest Hamming distance to this generated vector $h(x)$.

slides.title: – Given example 𝑥, create bit vector ℎ(𝑥) of length T where the ith bit:

The final classification is determined by identifying the class whose code has the smallest Hamming distance to this generated vector $h(x)$.

slides.title: Explaining why ensembles work
slides.summary: Explaining why ensembles work

slides.title: – Given a new data point x, what is the expected prediction error?
slides.summary: Given a new data point $x$ drawn independently and identically from an underlying distribution $p$, the goal is to compute the expected prediction error defined as $E_p[(y - h(x))^2]$. Here, $y$ represents the true label, $h(x)$ is the model's predicted label, and the expectation $E_p$ is taken across all possible training sets. This metric focuses on the squared error, which can be mathematically decomposed into a composition of terms, though students are not required to know the derivation.

slides.title: – Assume that the true function generating the true labels is 𝑓𝑥 and the
slides.summary: Assuming the true function generating labels is $f(x)$ and the average prediction of a hypothesis $h(x)$ is $\bar{h}(x)$, the expected squared error decomposes into three distinct components. This decomposition expresses the total expected error as the sum of Bias squared ($(\bar{h}(x) - f(x))^2$), Variance ($E_p[(h(x) - \bar{h}(x))^2]$), and irreducible Noise ($E_p[(y - f(x))^2]$). These terms collectively quantify how prediction accuracy is influenced by model approximation, sensitivity to training data variations, and inherent data randomness.

slides.title: – Assume that the true function generating the true labels is 𝑓𝑥 and the
slides.summary: Assuming $f(x)$ is the true function generating labels and $\bar{h}(x)$ is the average prediction of $h(x)$, the expected squared error decomposes into three components: bias squared, variance, and noise. Specifically, the total error equals the squared difference between the average prediction and the true target (bias), plus the expected squared deviation of individual predictions from their average (variance), plus the irreducible noise term. Bias is defined as the model's inability to represent the true target function.

slides.title: Faculteit, departement, dienst …
slides.summary: Bias is the gap between the true underlying function f(x) and the learned approximation h(x).

slides.title: – Inability to represent certain decision boundaries
slides.summary: Bias represents the inherent inability of a model to represent the true target function, often because its decision boundaries cannot match the data's shape, such as using a straight line for curved data. This error arises from incorrect assumptions, like Naïve Bayes failing when independence does not hold, or from classifiers that are "too global," such as single linear separators or small decision trees. Consequently, high bias indicates that the model is underfitting the data.

slides.title: – Assume that the true function generating the true labels is 𝑓𝑥 and the
slides.summary: Assuming $f(x)$ is the true function generating labels and $\bar{h}(x)$ is the average prediction of $h(x)$, the expected squared error decomposes into three components: bias squared, variance, and noise. Bias represents the model's inability to represent the true target, while variance captures fluctuations caused by variations in the data sample. This decomposition illustrates that total expected error arises from the sum of these distinct sources of uncertainty.

slides.title: Faculteit, departement, dienst …
slides.summary: The lecture introduces the concept of variance in the context of machine learning, visually contrasting the true underlying function $f(x)$ with a learned function $h(x)$. The slide highlights how the discrepancy between these two functions represents the variance component of model error.

slides.title: – Statistical sources
slides.summary: Statistical sources of variance arise when classifiers are "too local," causing them to overfit data by fitting small subsets or reacting sensitively to minor input changes. Key contributors include computational decisions on limited data (like fine-grained tree splits), algorithmic randomization (such as neural network weight initialization), and unstable learning algorithms where decision boundaries shift with single training examples. Consequently, high variance indicates a model that fits the training data well but deviates significantly from the true underlying function.

slides.title: – Assume that the true function generating the true labels is 𝑓𝑥 and the
slides.summary: Assuming $f(x)$ is the true function generating labels and $\bar{h}(x)$ is the average prediction of $h(x)$, the expected squared error decomposes into three components: bias squared, variance, and noise. Bias represents the model's inability to represent the true target, while variance captures fluctuations arising from variations in the data sample. Finally, noise reflects the inherent inability to distinguish between objects with different labels, contributing irreducibly to the total expected error.

slides.title: Faculteit, departement, dienst …
slides.summary: Observed points vary around the true function f(x). This random noise is irreducible error that even a correct model cannot predict exactly.

slides.title: – Inherent randomness
slides.summary: Noise in data arises from inherent randomness in genuinely stochastic processes like equipment failure or customer behavior. It also stems from unobserved variables where critical input features are missing, measurement errors caused by sensor disturbances or improper calibration, and ambiguous labels resulting from inconsistent expert assignments. These factors collectively mean the recorded data points are imperfect representations of reality.

slides.title: – Typically:
slides.summary: The bias-variance trade-off arises because bias occurs when a hypothesis class lacks good hypotheses to represent the correct target, while variance results from a class being too large and complex to fit excessive functions. Consequently, increasing expressiveness raises variance, whereas reducing it introduces higher bias. This fundamental tension is a standard interview concept in computer science and serves as a primary rationale for employing ensemble methods to balance model complexity.

slides.title: – Ensembles can address both bias and variance!
slides.summary: Ensembles address both bias and variance through distinct mechanisms in bagging and boosting. Theoretically, bagging reduces variance by varying training data via bootstrapping while keeping the model's bias constant; however, in practice, it can reduce both metrics depending on whether the classifier is high-bias or high-variance. Boosting primarily reduces bias in early iterations by adding decision surfaces to increase expressiveness, whereas later iterations empirically reduce variance, though the underlying reason remains an open question.

slides.title: – 3 possible coins
slides.summary: This slide introduces a Bayesian estimation problem involving three distinct coins (C1, C2, C3), each with specific probabilities of landing heads and prior selection probabilities. After selecting a coin based on its prior probability and observing a sequence of Heads followed by Tails in two flips, the objective is to calculate the conditional probability that the third flip will result in Heads, denoted as P(H|HT).

slides.title: – 3 possible coins
slides.summary: This slide presents a Bayesian estimation problem involving three coins (C1, C2, C3) with distinct probabilities of heads and prior selection probabilities. After observing a sequence of Heads then Tails, the likelihoods for each coin are calculated as 0.09 for C1, 0.25 for C2, and 0.09 for C3. The objective is to use these values to predict the probability of the third flip being heads, denoted as P(H|HT).

slides.title: – 3 possible coins
slides.summary: This slide illustrates a Bayesian estimation problem involving three coins with distinct head probabilities and prior selection chances. After observing a Heads-Tails sequence, the likelihoods for each coin are calculated and combined with their priors using Bayes' rule to determine posterior probabilities. The resulting normalized values show that while Coin 1 is highly unlikely (0.035), Coins 2 and 3 remain nearly equally probable candidates (0.481 and 0.485) for predicting the outcome of a third flip.

slides.title: – 3 possible coins
slides.summary: To predict the third flip after observing Heads-Tails, Bayes' rule updates the prior probabilities of three coins to posterior values: C1 (0.035), C2 (0.481), and C3 (0.485). Since the evidence strongly eliminates C1 but leaves C2 and C3 nearly equally likely, we cannot rely on a single coin's specific probability for the next flip. Instead, the prediction requires combining these posterior probabilities with their respective head probabilities to calculate the general likelihood of Heads given the observed sequence.

slides.title: – 3 possible coins
slides.summary: This slide illustrates a Bayesian estimation problem where one of three coins is selected based on prior probabilities, flipped twice to observe Heads-Tails (HT), and used to predict the probability of a third Head. By applying Bayes' rule, the likelihoods of observing HT for each coin are combined with their priors to calculate normalized posterior probabilities: P(C1|HT)≈0.035, P(C2|HT)≈0.481, and P(C3|HT)≈0.485. Since the specific coin remains unknown, the final prediction for the third flip is derived by summing the weighted probabilities of Heads across all coins, yielding approximately 0.68.

slides.title: – How can the learning algorithm select among set of (almost) equally good
slides.summary: To select among equally good hypotheses, the Bayes optimal classifier employs a weighted majority vote of all hypotheses, where weights correspond to their posterior probabilities. This approach is provably optimal as it minimizes the error rate, and ensemble learning serves to approximate this ideal by combining predictions to achieve better accuracy than any single trusted model.

slides.title: Faculteit, departement, dienst …
slides.summary: In the representation explanation, each learner operates within a specific hypothesis class that may not contain the true target function. Despite this limitation, ensemble averaging can approximate the actual target function with arbitrarily high accuracy by combining multiple learners. This approach effectively mitigates the risk of the target function lying outside any single considered hypothesis class.

slides.title: – Most learning algorithms search through hypothesis space to find one “good”
slides.summary: Most learning algorithms perform heuristic searches through huge or infinite hypothesis spaces to identify a good model, a process where learners risk becoming trapped in local minima. To mitigate this, repeating the search with random restarts allows the algorithm to escape suboptimal points and potentially reach the global optimum. This strategy parallels bagging, as both approaches leverage multiple attempts to overcome difficulties caused by noisy or ambiguous examples that might otherwise mislead a single search trajectory.

slides.title: Applications
slides.summary: Applications of ensemble learning.

slides.title: – The Netflix Prize Competition
slides.summary: The Netflix Prize Competition challenged participants to reduce the error of the Cinematch recommendation system by 10% using a dataset of 100 million ratings from 480,000 users and 17,700 films. The winning solution was a massive ensemble model that combined diverse techniques—including neighborhood models (kNN), bagged gradient boosted decision trees, temporal models, and matrix factorization—through stacking. This approach integrated five or six levels of learners, where individual predictions were fed into higher-level predictors to achieve superior accuracy.

slides.title: – Contextual ranking through XGBoost based on:
slides.summary: Contextual ranking utilizes XGBoost to synthesize five distinct signal categories for recommendation optimization. These inputs include collaborative signals reflecting similar listening patterns, content signals derived from audio or semantic track properties, and user-history signals capturing both long-term preferences and recent activity. The model further incorporates contextual signals regarding time, device, session, and current activity, alongside exploration systems designed to surface unfamiliar artists or newly released content.
